beef-and-vegetables-excluding-carrots-br.title: Beef and Vegetables without Carrots, Broccoli, Dark‑Green Leafy Greens

content.title: About
content.content: Thinly sliced beef is quickly stir‑fried with a mix of vegetables such as bell pepper, zucchini, cauliflower and onion, deliberately omitting carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens and potatoes. No soy‑based sauce is used, making the dish suitable for those avoiding soy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef provides highly bioavailable iron compared with plant sources.
Bell pepper and zucchini are rich in vitamin C, which enhances iron absorption from meat.
Skipping soy sauce reduces added glutamate, a common flavor enhancer.
High‑heat stir‑frying locks in beef juiciness while keeping vegetables crisp.
The recipe can be customized with different spices—cumin, paprika, ginger—to suit various cuisines.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef supplies complete animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and hemoglobin formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef is a good source of vitamin B12 for nervous system health and niacin for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Vitamin C and carotenoids in bell pepper and zucchini help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Excluding potatoes and carrots makes the dish suitable for low‑carb eating patterns.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Large portions of beef can raise cholesterol levels; choose lean cuts when possible.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Overcooking vegetables
items.content: Excessive stir‑frying can degrade vitamins and create harmful compounds.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice beef thinly, stir‑fry on high heat for 2‑3 minutes, then add the vegetables (bell pepper, zucchini, cauliflower, onion). Season with salt, pepper and your favorite spices. Cook, stirring, until vegetables are tender‑crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat with a splash of water or broth to restore moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Biscuit cheese is a soft, creamy dairy product made from milk and cream, with added eggs and sugar, giving it a light, airy texture similar to a biscuit. It has a mild buttery flavor with a hint of sweetness and is commonly used in desserts and pastries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Biscuit cheese originated in Europe in the 19th century as a substitute for traditional curd in confectionery.
It is often used as a filling for rolls, cakes, and eclairs.
Unlike aged cheeses, biscuit cheese requires no maturation and is ready to eat immediately after production.
In some countries it is called “cheese biscuit” or “cream cheese” in a biscuit form.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Biscuit cheese provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Protein supports tissue repair and helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamins B2 and B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Compared with most hard cheeses, it contains less salt.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains lactose, so people with intolerance should limit consumption.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sugar is added for sweetness, making it unsuitable for low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to casein.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Biscuit cheese can be enjoyed on its own as a dessert, spread on bread, used as a filling for cakes, rolls, eclairs, and other pastries. It is also incorporated into creams and mousses to give a light, airy texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 2 °C–6 °C in its original packaging. Once opened, it is best consumed within 7–10 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or off‑color.

content.title: About
content.content: Cookies and brownies are baked goods made from flour, sugar, eggs, and butter. The NS (no gluten) version uses gluten‑free flour, and the icing adds a sweet, glossy finish. This product works as a snack, dessert, or coffee accompaniment.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brownies originated in the United States in the early 20th century and quickly became popular for their dense, fudgy texture.
The NS gluten‑free version allows people with celiac disease to enjoy the treat safely.
Icing is often made from chocolate, butter, and a splash of cream, giving it a smooth, shiny appearance.
Cookies can be crisp or soft depending on the recipe and baking time.
Combining cookie and brownie in one product is a common bakery technique to create multi‑textured desserts.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Provides quick‑acting carbohydrates that replenish energy stores.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Chocolate icing is rich in flavonoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Flour and cocoa powder contribute a modest amount of iron, supporting blood formation.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: Sugar and chocolate stimulate serotonin production, improving mood.

items.title: Gluten‑free (NS)
items.content: Suitable for individuals with gluten intolerance, reducing inflammation risk.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Icing often contains milk and butter, which can trigger reactions in dairy‑allergic individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may lead to weight gain and elevated blood glucose.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The product is calorie‑rich, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Trans‑fat presence
items.content: Some recipes use partially hydrogenated oils; choose trans‑fat‑free versions when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie and brownie as a standalone treat, incorporate them into cakes, ice cream, or use them as a base for ice‑cream sandwiches. Icing can also be drizzled over other desserts or used as a dip.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 5 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 2 weeks) or freeze (up to 3 months).

content.title: About
content.content: A whole boiled egg without added salt is a fully cooked chicken egg, boiled hard or soft. The egg retains most of its nutrients, and the lack of salt makes it suitable for low‑sodium diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable and nutrient‑dense foods worldwide.
The shell is mainly calcium carbonate and can be used as a garden fertilizer.
Boiled eggs can be kept in the refrigerator for up to a week if left in the shell.
Eggs are commonly used as a binding and emulsifying agent in cooking.
Vitamin D content rises when hens have adequate exposure to sunlight.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A large egg provides about 6 g of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, riboflavin (B2) and biotin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains choline
items.content: Choline is important for liver function and brain development, especially during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidants present
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in the yolk protect the eyes from age‑related macular degeneration.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: No added salt makes the egg suitable for people monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Salmonella risk
items.content: Undercooked eggs can harbor Salmonella bacteria; ensure eggs are fully cooked.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: The yolk contains about 186 mg of cholesterol; people with hypercholesterolemia should limit intake.

items.title: Overconsumption
items.content: Eating too many eggs can lead to excess calories and protein.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled eggs can be eaten plain as a snack, sliced into salads, added to sandwiches, or used in dishes like deviled eggs. They are convenient to keep in the fridge and peel when needed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store boiled eggs in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C, preferably in their shells, in a sealed container. Consume within 5‑7 days. Discard any egg with an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned salmon is made from selected salmon fillets that are packed in their own juices or oil and sealed in airtight tins. The product retains a high level of protein, omega‑3 fatty acids, and B‑vitamins, offering a tender texture and a distinct marine flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salmon is one of the most valuable commercial fish, rich in EPA and DHA omega‑3 fatty acids.
Canning preserves the nutritional qualities of the fish for up to 3‑5 years without added preservatives.
Traditionally canned in Scandinavian countries, salmon is a staple of the regional diet.
The natural aroma of salmon is often retained thanks to minimal use of spices and salt.
Canned salmon is convenient for salads, sandwiches, pastas, and as a quick protein source in outdoor settings.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3 supports cardiovascular health, lowers triglyceride levels, and has anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Salmon protein is easily digestible and aids muscle and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B12 and B6 support the nervous system and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and iodine
items.content: Selenium protects cells from oxidative stress, while iodine is essential for thyroid function.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Makes it suitable for low‑carb and keto diets.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to seafood may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned salmon is often salted; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Bisphenol A (BPA)
items.content: Some cans may be lined with BPA, an endocrine disruptor; choose BPA‑free packaging when possible.

items.title: Potential parasites
items.content: Thermal processing during canning eliminates most parasites, but it is important to respect expiration dates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned salmon can be eaten straight from the tin, added to salads, pasta, rice rolls, or spread on whole‑grain bread. For a milder taste, it is often mixed with a splash of lemon juice, dill, or mustard.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened tins in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer the salmon to an airtight container and consume within 2‑3 days, kept refrigerated.

content.title: About
content.content: White fish is a generic term for several marine and freshwater species with a mild, light-colored flesh. Product NFS (1123) is a blend of different white fish species processed according to safe food standards, without artificial preservatives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The white fish blend often includes cod, pollock, hake and sea bass.
White fish is high in protein and low in fat, making it popular in diet nutrition.
Unlike red fish, white fish has a more neutral flavor, allowing it to be used in a wide range of dishes.
The NFS (Not From Salmon) label indicates the product contains no salmon or its derivatives.
Fresh white fish fillet can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 2 days, frozen for up to 6 months.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: White fish provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The low amount of saturated fat makes it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports the nervous system and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium has antioxidant properties and supports immune function.

items.title: Provides iodine
items.content: Iodine is important for normal thyroid gland function.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Risk of heavy metal contamination
items.content: Certain fish species can accumulate mercury and other toxins; varied consumption is recommended.

items.title: Not suitable for infants under 1 year
items.content: Small bones may pose a choking hazard for young children.

items.title: Sodium content in processed products
items.content: If the fish is pre‑salted, monitor overall sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: White fish can be baked, boiled, grilled, or steamed. It works well in soups, salads, fish cakes, and sushi. Before cooking, remove any bones and rinse the fillet under cold water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh fish in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for no more than 2 days. Keep frozen fish at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen fish in the refrigerator or under cold running water before use.
